sections.html:
A seller in Knox County will typically deal with three offices. The County Treasurer, in the courthouse in Galesburg, mails the bills and takes the money. The county Assessment Office, 309-345-3845, runs exemptions and hands out Board of Review forms. Township assessors set the values. Tax sale certificates and redemption sit with the County Clerk.

Assessing is split three ways. One assessor covers the North District: Rio, Ontario, Walnut Grove, Lynn, Henderson, Sparta, Copley, Victoria, Persifer and Truro townships. Another covers the South District: Galesburg, Knox, Cedar, Orange, Haw Creek, Elba, Indian Point, Chestnut, Maquon and Salem. The City of Galesburg township has its own assessor, so the right call depends on where the parcel sits.

Galesburg is both the seat and the biggest city of Knox County, in west central Illinois. Population is sliding, from 49,967 in the 2020 count to an estimated 47,767 in July 2025. The median home value is $111,900, 70.8% of households own their homes, and median income is $57,030.

Where values are this low, even a modest bill takes a real share of a house's worth, so look at the assessment before you list.

Taxes are payable in two installments, around July 1 and September 1. Knox County mails one bill a year with a detachable stub for each installment, so read the dates on your current bill or ask the Treasurer.

Knox County late penalty by date
Penalty startsFirst installmentSecond installment
July 21.50%Not yet due
August 23.00%Not yet due
September 24.50%1.50%
October 26.00%3.00%
November 27.50%4.50%

The charge is 1.5% each month, applies in full rather than by the day, and begins the morning after a due date. A bill that never arrives does not excuse the tax (35 ILCS 200/20-15).

The Treasurer takes payment several ways, and the detachable stub has to go with it:

  • Mail a check or deliver it to the Treasurer's Office, made out to Knox County Collector. A mailed check's cancelled copy is your receipt.
  • Leave a check in a courthouse drop box, one on Tompkins Street by the north curb and one at the parking lot exit. No envelopes are supplied.
  • Take it to a local bank in the county (Wells Fargo is excluded at its own request).
  • Use a credit or debit card and pay a fee of 2.35%, with a $2.95 minimum.

A postmark counts if the payment goes out before the tax sale. Drop box items collected at 8:30 each morning are posted to the day before. If a lender pays from escrow, the county still expects the owner to watch those payments.

Assessors value property as of each January 1, aiming for 33.33% of fair cash value and drawing on three years of sales. Equalization factors follow. For 2026 they were 1.0724 in Galesburg Township, 1.0758 for the City of Galesburg, 1.0132 in Rio, Walnut Grove, Henderson and Persifer, and 1.0125 in Ontario, Sparta and Copley. Lynn, Truro, Victoria, Elba and Salem were general assessment townships that year.

The formula for a bill takes the final equalized assessed value, subtracts exemptions, and multiplies what remains by the tax rate. To test your own figure, divide the assessment by 0.3333 and compare that with a realistic sale price.

Before the 2026 adjustments, the three-year median assessment level measured 32.92% in the North District, 31.08% in the South District and 31.76% in the City of Galesburg, which is why the factors push values upward. Farmland follows a separate state formula, and its factor was 1.00.

Talk to the township assessor first. If that does not settle it, put a written appeal in front of the Board of Review. It must argue the property's value, not the size of the tax. The filing period opens in mid-September and closes in the second half of October, ending at 4 p.m. on the last day. Each year brings new forms, and older ones are refused.

  • Support the appeal with facts, such as an independent appraisal or sales of comparable homes.
  • The Board answers with a notice carrying an informal decision.
  • To contest it, return your acceptance of a formal hearing within ten days of the notice.
  • Thirty days after a final Board decision is the limit for going to the Property Tax Appeal Board.

The Board of Review meets as needed rather than on a fixed calendar. For the current forms and window, call the Assessment Office at 309-345-3845.

Exemption forms and instructions are on the county's assessment pages, and the Treasurer's page summarizes the main ones:

  • Owner-occupied homestead: a reduction of up to $6,000 in equalized assessed value.
  • Senior homestead for owners 65 and older: $5,000 off.
  • Senior assessment freeze: holds the taxable value for owners 65 and older. The Treasurer lists household income of $65,000 or less, and the assessment office shows $75,000 for 2026.
  • Home improvement: assessed value of up to $25,000 exempt for four years.

Other exemptions cover returning veteran, disabled person and disabled veteran cases. Applications are requested by September 30 each year and accepted until December 31. A buyer who moves in should contact the assessment office after the next January 1 to confirm the exemption is on the parcel.

sections.h2: Delinquent taxes and the tax sale
sections.html:
Knox County runs one tax sale a year, usually in mid-November, and every delinquent tax is offered. A list of delinquent taxes is printed in local newspapers each mid-October. Under Public Act 104-0553, the county now acquires all delinquent real estate taxes itself as trustee for the taxing districts. That trustee then auctions parcels it has taken to deed.

Tax sale certificates are handled by the County Clerk's Office, 309-345-6753. The Treasurer will not give legal advice about delinquent taxes.

If tax is outstanding when you sell, ask the Treasurer what is owed and settle it at closing from your proceeds. Have the title company confirm with the Clerk that no certificate has been issued on the parcel. A cash sale skips a lender's underwriting, so these two checks are often what set the closing date. For a buyer who plans to live in the house, remind them to ask about the homestead exemption after the next January 1.

faqs.q: What dates does Knox County collect real estate tax?
faqs.a: Taxes come due in two installments, around July 1 and September 1. The Treasurer mails one annual bill with a stub for each installment, so read the dates on your own bill.

faqs.q: What late fee does Knox County charge?
faqs.a: The Treasurer adds 1.5% per month to the unpaid amount, with no proration, starting the day after a due date.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my assessment?
faqs.a: The Board of Review filing period opens in mid-September and closes in the second half of October, and the Board may not accept complaints afterward. Call the Assessment Office at 309-345-3845 for the current window.

faqs.q: Where do I send a property tax payment?
faqs.a: The Treasurer's Office in the Knox County courthouse in Galesburg takes mail and walk-in payments. Drop boxes, most local banks and card payments are also options, and checks go to the Knox County Collector.

faqs.q: When does Knox County hold the tax sale?
faqs.a: It is usually held in mid-November, following a mid-October newspaper list of delinquent taxes. The County Clerk handles the certificates.
